fact_check_evidence: Scientific American ('Right Side Up', 2008): "The lens in your eye casts an upside-down image on your retina, but you see the world upright." (https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/right-side-up-2008-05/)

claim: Each eye has a blind spot where the optic nerve leaves the retina, a patch with no rods or cones; we rarely notice it because the two eyes' views overlap and the brain fills in or ignores the gap.
fact_check_evidence: All About Vision (Optic disc): the only spot on the retina with no rods or cones, where optic nerve fibers exit the eye; the brain fills in the missing information. (https://www.allaboutvision.com/eye-care/eye-anatomy/eye-structure/optic-disc/)

claim: The retina has two kinds of light-sensing cell: rods, which provide vision in low light, and cones, which provide vision in bright light, including color vision.
fact_check_evidence: AAO (Parts of the Eye): rods handle black-and-white vision, while cones perceive color. (https://www.aao.org/eye-health/anatomy/parts-of-eye)

claim: There are three types of cone, each with a pigment most sensitive to particular wavelengths of light, and the brain combines input from all three to produce color vision.
fact_check_evidence: AAO (What is color blindness?): "There are three types of cones that see color: red, green and blue." The brain uses input from these cone cells to determine color perception. (https://www.aao.org/eye-health/diseases/what-is-color-blindness)

claim: The most common type of color vision deficiency makes it hard to tell the difference between red and green.
fact_check_evidence: AAO (What is color blindness?): color blindness usually happens between greens and reds, and occasionally blues; Colour Blind Awareness names red/green as the most common forms. (https://www.aao.org/eye-health/diseases/what-is-color-blindness https://www.colourblindawareness.org/colour-blindness/)

claim: Among people with Northern European ancestry, red-green color blindness affects about 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women.
fact_check_evidence: Colour Blind Awareness: colour blindness "affects approximately 1 in 12 men (8%) and 1 in 200 women." NEI states about 1 in 12 men; its current page gives no figure for women. (https://www.colourblindawareness.org/colour-blindness/ https://www.nei.nih.gov/eye-health-information/eye-conditions-and-diseases/color-blindness)

claim: The genes for red-green color blindness are passed down on the X chromosome; males have one X chromosome, so one copy is enough, while females must have the gene on both X chromosomes.
fact_check_evidence: MedlinePlus Genetics: OPN1LW and OPN1MW are on the X chromosome; in males one genetic change is sufficient, while in females a change would have to occur in both copies. (https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/condition/color-vision-deficiency/)

claim: In 1794 the chemist John Dalton described his own and his brother's color vision to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society, the first published account of color blindness.
fact_check_evidence: Royal Society: Dalton's account to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1794 is the first recorded description of colour blindness; his brother saw as he did. (https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/diversity-inclusion/case-studies/scientists-with-disabilities/john-dalton/)

claim: In 1794 the chemist John Dalton described his own and his brother's color vision to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society, the first published account of color blindness.
fact_check_evidence: Royal Society: Dalton's account to the Manchester Literary and Philosophical Society in 1794 is the first recorded description of colour blindness; his brother saw as he did. (https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/diversity-inclusion/case-studies/scientists-with-disabilities/john-dalton/)

claim: Dalton guessed that the jelly-like fluid in his eyes was tinted blue and asked for his eyes to be examined after his death; in 1844 the fluid was found to be colorless.
fact_check_evidence: Royal Society: Dalton thought his vitreous humour had an abnormal blue tint; a post-mortem examination of his eyes in 1844, performed at his request, found the contents "perfectly colourless". (https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/diversity-inclusion/case-studies/scientists-with-disabilities/john-dalton/)

claim: In 1995, DNA from Dalton's preserved eye showed he lacked the gene for the medium-wavelength (green-sensitive) cone pigment.
fact_check_evidence: Hektoen International: DNA from Dalton's eye fragments showed a single LW (red) gene and no MW (green) gene; he was a deuteranope. Royal Society dates the DNA analysis to 1995. (Hunt et al., Science 1995.) (https://hekint.org/2017/01/22/john-daltons-eyes-a-history-of-the-eye-and-color-vision-part-two/ https://royalsociety.org/about-us/who-we-are/diversity-inclusion/case-studies/scientists-with-disabilities/john-dalton/ https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.7863342)

claim: Refractive errors happen when the shape of the eye keeps light from focusing correctly on the retina, for example when the eyeball is too long or too short or the cornea is misshaped.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Myopia): the myopic eye is usually longer than normal from front to rear, so images of distant objects focus in front of the retina. (https://www.britannica.com/science/myopia)

claim: In nearsightedness (myopia), light focuses in front of the retina instead of on it, often because the eyeball is too long, so far-away objects look blurry.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Myopia): the resting eye focuses the image of a distant object at a point in front of the retina; the eye is usually longer than normal. (https://www.britannica.com/science/myopia)

claim: In farsightedness (hyperopia), light focuses behind the retina instead of on it, often because the eyeball is too short, so nearby objects look blurry.
fact_check_evidence: AAO lens figure: in hyperopia parallel rays are focused posterior to the macula; Britannica (Hyperopia) describes images projected behind rather than on the retina. (https://www.aao.org/education/image/concave-convex-cylinder-lenses-2 https://www.britannica.com/science/hyperopia)

claim: A concave lens, thinner in the middle, spreads light rays apart and corrects nearsightedness; a convex lens, thicker in the middle, brings rays together and corrects farsightedness.
fact_check_evidence: All About Vision: a concave lens is thinner at the center and diverges light so it focuses further back, on the retina; CK-12: a convex lens converges light rays to correct hypermetropia. (https://www.allaboutvision.com/conditions/myopia/how-lenses-correct-nearsightedness/ https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physics/double-convex-lenses/which-type-of-lens-is-used-to-correct-myopia-and-which-type-is-used-to-correct-hypermetropia/)

(https://www.allaboutvision.com/conditions/myopia/how-lenses-correct-nearsightedness/ https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physics/double-convex-lenses/which-type-of-lens-is-used-to-correct-myopia-and-which-type-is-used-to-correct-hypermetropia/)

(https://www.allaboutvision.com/conditions/myopia/how-lenses-correct-nearsightedness/ https://www.ck12.org/flexi/physics/double-convex-lenses/which-type-of-lens-is-used-to-correct-myopia-and-which-type-is-used-to-correct-hypermetropia/)

claim: A contact lens is a thin artificial lens worn on the surface of the eye to correct refractive errors, as a substitute for eyeglasses.
fact_check_evidence: FDA (Contact Lenses): contact lenses can be used to correct myopia (nearsightedness), hyperopia (farsightedness), astigmatism and presbyopia; NEI lists eyeglasses or contact lenses as the common treatments. (https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/consumer-products/contact-lenses https://www.nei.nih.gov/eye-health-information/eye-conditions-and-diseases/nearsightedness-myopia)

claim: The earliest eyeglasses, which in Europe first appeared in Italy, had convex lenses to help farsighted people.
fact_check_evidence: Salus University: Italian monks crafted the first ground lenses in the 13th century; these reading aids had a convex lens and were used to help far-sighted individuals read. (https://www.salus.edu/news-stories/2019/03/the-quest-for-clearer-vision-the-history-of-eyeglasses.html)

claim: Raphael's portrait of Pope Leo X, painted in the late 1510s (dated 1517 to about 1519), shows the nearsighted pope holding a concave lens, an early picture of a lens for myopia.
fact_check_evidence: Hektoen International (Medicean optics): the concave lens the Pope holds in Raphael's portrait (dated 1518 to 1519) shows he was highly myopic; the lens is measured at about minus 12 diopters. (https://hekint.org/2020/12/09/medicean-optics-an-analysis-of-raffaellos-portrait-of-pope-leo-x-and-two-cardinals/)

claim: Hearing turns sound waves in the air into electrical signals, which the auditory nerve carries to the brain.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Ear): the ear converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses in the organ of Corti, which travel to the brain. (https://www.britannica.com/science/ear)

claim: Sound waves travel down the ear canal to the eardrum, which vibrates and passes the vibrations to three tiny middle-ear bones, the malleus, incus and stapes, which amplify them.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Ear): the outer ear guides sound to the tympanic membrane; the malleus, incus and stapes (the auditory ossicles) transmit sound to the inner ear. (https://www.britannica.com/science/ear)

claim: The stapes, or stirrup, is the smallest of the three middle-ear bones and is shaped like a stirrup.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Ear) lists the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil) and stapes (stirrup) as the auditory ossicles; NIDCD names the same three tiny bones. (https://www.britannica.com/science/ear https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/how-do-we-hear)

claim: The middle-ear bones pass the vibrations to the cochlea, a snail-shaped, fluid-filled structure in the inner ear.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Ear): the snail-shell-like cochlea contains the sensory organ of hearing. (https://www.britannica.com/science/ear)

claim: In the cochlea, vibrations set off a traveling wave on the basilar membrane; hair cells near the wide end detect high-pitched sounds, and those near the center detect low-pitched sounds.
fact_check_evidence: UTHealth Neuroscience Online and Cochlea.eu (search results): hair cells at the base of the cochlea are tuned to high frequencies and those toward the apex to low frequencies (tonotopy). (https://nba.uth.tmc.edu/neuroscience/m/s2/chapter12.html https://www.cochlea.eu/en/cochlea/function/)

claim: As hair cells move, tiny bristles on top (stereocilia) bend, opening channels that let chemicals rush in and create an electrical signal.
fact_check_evidence: NIDCD Noise-Induced Hearing Loss page repeats the mechanism: stereocilia bump against an overlying structure and bend, opening pore-like channels. (https://www.nidcd.nih.gov/health/noise-induced-hearing-loss)

claim: Unlike the hair cells of birds and amphibians, human hair cells don't grow back; most noise-induced hearing loss is caused by their damage and death.
fact_check_evidence: Stanford Medicine: destroyed hair cells in humans are "permanently powerless to help us hear", but in birds, amphibians and reptiles these cells grow back. (https://med.stanford.edu/stanmed/listening/scientists-hope-cure-hearing-loss-studying-birds)

claim: The part of the inner ear that handles balance is the vestibular system, or labyrinth, a maze-like structure of bone and soft tissue that sits beside the cochlea.
fact_check_evidence: Cleveland Clinic (Vestibular system): the vestibular system in the inner ear, with its semicircular canals, utricle and saccule, senses motion and head position; Britannica (Ear) places the vestibular apparatus in the inner ear alongside the cochlea. (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/vestibular-system https://www.britannica.com/science/ear)

claim: Three fluid-filled semicircular canals, looped at roughly right angles to one another, sense head rotation: when the head turns, the fluid moves and bends hair cells, signaling which way it turned.
fact_check_evidence: Cleveland Clinic: the semicircular canals are three tubes that detect rotational head movements; moving endolymph shifts the hair cells. Medscape: the canals lie at about 90 degrees to one another. (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/vestibular-system https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/883956-overview)

claim: In the utricle and saccule, hair cells sit under a gel holding tiny grains of calcium carbonate; gravity pulls on the grains, telling the brain whether the head is upright, tilted back or lying down.
fact_check_evidence: Cleveland Clinic: the macula's hair cells extend into a gelatin-like substance filled with calcium crystals called otoconia; Medscape: the otolith organs detect head position relative to gravity. (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/vestibular-system https://emedicine.medscape.com/article/883956-overview)

claim: The sense of balance relies on signals to the brain from the eyes, the inner ears, and the muscles and touch sensors in the legs.
fact_check_evidence: Cleveland Clinic (Vestibular system): the brain integrates vestibular data with sensory information from the eyes, muscles and joints. (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/body/vestibular-system)

claim: After you spin and stop, the fluid in the semicircular canals keeps moving, so the inner ear signals motion while the eyes show you are still, and you feel dizzy.
fact_check_evidence: Popular Science: "Even though you stopped, that fluid is still moving"; the ears signal motion while the eyes register stillness, producing dizziness. (https://www.popsci.com/why-do-i-feel-dizzy-after-spinning/)

claim: The most widely accepted explanation of motion sickness is sensory conflict: in a ship cabin with no outside view, the inner ear reports motion while the eyes suggest you are not moving.
fact_check_evidence: Cleveland Clinic (Motion sickness): it happens when the brain gets conflicting messages from the parts of the body that sense motion; being below deck on a boat is a common trigger. (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/12782-motion-sickness)

claim: Taste cells are clustered in taste buds on the tongue and the roof of the mouth and along the lining of the throat.
fact_check_evidence: Smithsonian: areas of the mouth containing taste buds include several parts of the tongue, the soft palate on the roof of the mouth, and the throat. (https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/neat-and-tidy-map-tastes-tongue-you-learned-school-all-wrong-180963407/)

claim: Taste cells respond to at least five basic tastes: sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami, the savory taste of glutamate, found in foods such as broth, meat extracts and some cheeses.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Umami): umami is the savory taste, one of the five fundamental tastes with sweet, sour, salty and bitter, produced by glutamate among other compounds; cheese is a rich source. (https://www.britannica.com/topic/umami)

claim: The tongue map is a misconception: taste cells for different tastes are scattered across the tongue, and every area with taste buds senses all the basic tastes.
fact_check_evidence: Gizmodo ('Why did we believe in the tongue map?'): all areas of the tongue can detect all tastes; Virginia Collings's 1970s retest found the sensitivity differences made little to no practical difference. (https://gizmodo.com/baffling-science-hoaxes-why-did-we-believe-in-the-tong-5927877)

claim: The tongue map is a misconception: taste cells for different tastes are scattered across the tongue, and every area with taste buds senses all the basic tastes.
fact_check_evidence: Gizmodo ('Why did we believe in the tongue map?'): all areas of the tongue can detect all tastes; Virginia Collings's 1970s retest found the sensitivity differences made little to no practical difference. (https://gizmodo.com/baffling-science-hoaxes-why-did-we-believe-in-the-tong-5927877)

claim: The tongue map grew out of a 1901 study by David Hanig that found only tiny differences in taste sensitivity around the tongue, redrawn in the 1940s by Harvard psychologist Edwin Boring.
fact_check_evidence: Gizmodo: D. P. Hanig's 1901 paper found areas of the tongue slightly more sensitive to different tastes; Harvard's Edwin Boring ran with the idea in his 1942 book, and different sensitivities became total ability. (https://gizmodo.com/baffling-science-hoaxes-why-did-we-believe-in-the-tong-5927877)

claim: Smell comes from olfactory sensory neurons in a small patch of tissue high inside the nose; odors reach them through the nostrils and, as you chew, through a channel from the roof of the throat to the nose.
fact_check_evidence: Arizona State University, Ask A Biologist: when we chew and swallow, odor molecules go up behind the palate through the back of the nasal cavity to odor receptors. (https://askabiologist.asu.edu/smell-taste)

claim: Flavor combines the basic tastes with sensations of heat, cold and texture and a food's aroma; it is flavor that tells a pear from an apple, and when a cold blocks the nose, food tastes bland.
fact_check_evidence: Ask A Biologist: the flavor of some foods comes primarily from their smell, and food doesn't taste the same with a stuffed-up nose. (https://askabiologist.asu.edu/smell-taste)

claim: Somatosensory receptors fall into four categories: mechanoreceptors (touch and pressure), thermoreceptors (temperature), nociceptors (pain) and chemoreceptors.
fact_check_evidence: Kenhub (Sensory receptors) describes mechanoreceptors (pressure, vibration, stretch), thermoreceptors (temperature), nociceptors (harmful stimuli, felt as pain) and chemoreceptors (chemical stimuli). (https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/physiology/sensory-receptors)

claim: Free nerve endings are the most common nerve endings in the skin and respond to painful stimuli, to hot and cold, and to light touch.
fact_check_evidence: Kenhub: free nerve endings detect pain and temperature in the dermis and also function in touch; ScienceDirect Topics (search result): free nerve endings are receptors for pain, temperature and crude touch. (https://www.kenhub.com/en/library/physiology/sensory-receptors https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/neuroscience/free-nerve-ending)

claim: Touch receptors are denser in hairless skin such as the fingertips and lips, which is more sensitive, and less dense in hairy skin such as the arms, legs and torso.
fact_check_evidence: UTHealth Neuroscience Online and Nursing Times (search results): touch discrimination is most acute on the fingers and face, where receptor density is highest, and poor on the back. (https://nba.uth.tmc.edu/neuroscience/m/s2/chapter02.html https://www.nursingtimes.net/neurology/the-senses-4-touch-physiology-of-the-sensation-and-perception-of-touch-13-12-2022/)

claim: Pain is a vital signal that helps people avoid danger; people born unable to feel pain can still tell hot from cold but not that a drink is burning their tongue, have more injuries and may live shorter lives.
fact_check_evidence: NORD (Congenital insensitivity to pain): pain normally acts as a warning signal; people with CIP have fractures that may go unnoticed and burns from impaired temperature sensation. (https://rarediseases.org/rare-diseases/congenital-insensitivity-to-pain-cip/)

claim: Channelopathy-associated congenital insensitivity to pain is a rare condition caused by variants in a single gene, SCN9A.
fact_check_evidence: Nature (Cox et al. 2006, 'An SCN9A channelopathy causes congenital inability to experience pain'); NORD lists SCN9A among the genes behind CIP subtypes. (https://www.nature.com/articles/nature05413 https://rarediseases.org/rare-diseases/congenital-insensitivity-to-pain-cip/)

claim: David Julius and Ardem Patapoutian shared the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering receptors for temperature and touch.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (David Julius): he received the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, shared with Ardem Patapoutian, for discovering temperature-sensing receptors. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/David-Julius)

claim: In the late 1990s, Julius used capsaicin, the chili pepper compound that causes a burning feeling, to find TRPV1, a sensor in nerve endings that is switched on by heat at temperatures felt as painful.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (David Julius): Julius identified TRPV1, an ion channel that responds to heat and to capsaicin, the compound in chili peppers. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/David-Julius)

claim: Julius and Patapoutian each independently used menthol to identify TRPM8, a sensor switched on by cold.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Julius; Patapoutian): both are credited with the cold-sensing ion channel TRPM8, the first cold receptor discovered. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/David-Julius https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ardem-Patapoutian)

claim: Patapoutian discovered Piezo2, a pressure sensor that is essential for the sense of touch and plays a key role in sensing body position and movement.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica (Ardem Patapoutian): his work showed Piezo2 is the primary transducer for touch, converting mechanical force into neuronal signals. (https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ardem-Patapoutian)

claim: An optical illusion is a perception that contradicts objective reality; illusions can come from light or poor lighting, from the eye itself, and from how the brain processes visual information.
fact_check_evidence: EBSCO Research Starters (Muller-Lyer illusion): the illusion plays on differences in people's visual systems, showing perception depends on how the brain interprets visual data; the Illusions Index describes the visual system deceived by context. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/muller-lyer-illusion/ https://www.illusionsindex.org/i/mueller-lyer/)

claim: In the Muller-Lyer illusion, published by Franz Carl Muller-Lyer in 1889, two lines of equal length look different: the one with fins flaring outward at its ends looks longer than the one capped with arrowheads.
fact_check_evidence: EBSCO Research Starters: Franz Carl Muller-Lyer devised the illusion in 1889; two lines of the same length look different because of the arrows at their ends, one set pointing outward and one inward. (https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/history/muller-lyer-illusion/)

claim: In Edward Adelson's 1995 checker-shadow illusion, a square in a cylinder's shadow looks much lighter than a square outside it, although both are exactly the same shade of grey.
fact_check_evidence: Michael Bach (Optical Illusions): Ted Adelson published the illusion in 1995; square B appears brighter, but isolated, the two squares have identical luminance. (https://michaelbach.de/ot/lum-adelsonCheckShadow/)

claim: The visual system estimates where the light in a scene comes from and judges each surface's own shade regardless of shadow, which keeps objects looking the same color as lighting changes; on a flat picture, that correction misleads.
fact_check_evidence: Michael Bach: interpreted as a 3-D scene, the visual system estimates a lighting vector and uses it to judge the material, irrespective of shadow. (https://michaelbach.de/ot/lum-adelsonCheckShadow/)

claim: Sensory receptors are specialized cells that respond to particular kinds of stimuli, and converting a stimulus's energy into a nerve signal is called transduction.
fact_check_evidence: Noba (Sensation and Perception): transduction is the conversion of one form of energy into another, such as light or sound waves into electrical signals the brain can process. (https://nobaproject.com/modules/sensation-and-perception)

claim: Sensation is a sensory receptor detecting a stimulus; perception is the way the brain organizes, interprets and consciously experiences that sensory information.
fact_check_evidence: Noba: perception is the psychological process of making sense of the stimuli, distinct from sensation. (https://nobaproject.com/modules/sensation-and-perception)

claim: Sensory adaptation: we often stop perceiving stimuli that stay relatively constant over long periods, such as a light flashing steadily outside a window.
fact_check_evidence: Noba: when a stimulus is constant and unchanging, we experience sensory adaptation; the example is a car radio volume that seems normal after a long drive. (https://nobaproject.com/modules/sensation-and-perception)

claim: Skin is the body's largest organ; it covers the whole body and acts as a protective barrier against the outside world.
fact_check_evidence: MedlinePlus Components of skin: about 6 pounds of skin covering 18 square feet in the average adult. (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/anatomyvideos/000029.htm)

claim: The skin's primary role is to serve as a physical barrier that protects the body from foreign organisms such as germs.
fact_check_evidence: MedlinePlus Immune response lists skin among the barriers that keep harmful materials from entering the body. (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/article/000821.htm)

claim: Skin has three layers: the epidermis of closely packed epithelial cells on top, the dermis with blood vessels, hair follicles and sweat glands, and the mostly fatty hypodermis.
fact_check_evidence: MedlinePlus Components of skin: epidermis outer layer, dermis with blood vessels and receptors, hypodermis of fat tissue. (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/anatomyvideos/000029.htm)

claim: An adult's skin covers about 1.8 square meters.
fact_check_evidence: MedlinePlus: about 18 square feet of skin in an average adult (about 1.7 square meters), consistent with about 1.8 m2. (https://medlineplus.gov/ency/anatomyvideos/000029.htm)

claim: The outermost layer of the epidermis, the stratum corneum, is made of dry, dead cells filled with keratin that help keep microbes out and stop water loss.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica human skin: the tough, dead cells of the outer epidermal surface (corneal layer) serve as a physical barrier. (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-skin)

claim: Keratin is a tough fibrous protein that gives hair, nails and skin their hardness and water resistance.
fact_check_evidence: MedlinePlus Genetics (KRT genes): keratins are tough, fibrous proteins forming the framework of cells of the skin, hair and nails. (https://medlineplus.gov/genetics/gene/krt5/)

claim: New epidermal cells are made at the base of the epidermis and pushed upward, dying as they go; the outer layer is replaced about every 4 weeks.
fact_check_evidence: Britannica: corneal-layer cells are continually replaced by cells produced in the basal layer; PMC4523269 describes the epidermis as fully renewing about every 4 weeks. (https://www.britannica.com/science/human-skin https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4523269/)

claim: The skin surface is cool, dry and slightly acidic (pH on average below 5), and that acidity holds back harmful bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus.
fact_check_evidence: PMC7167948: the acid mantle has a pH of 4 to 6, and most human-pathogen bacteria are inhibited by the acidic milieu on normal skin. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7167948/)

claim: The skin surface is cool, dry and slightly acidic (pH on average below 5), and that acidity holds back harmful bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus.
fact_check_evidence: PMC7167948: the acid mantle has a pH of 4 to 6, and most human-pathogen bacteria are inhibited by the acidic milieu on normal skin. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7167948/)

claim: Oil glands in the skin make an oil that keeps skin from drying out and kills bacteria.
fact_check_evidence: PMC3057125: sebum free fatty acids have antibacterial activity and are partly responsible for the direct antimicrobial activity of the skin surface. (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3057125/)

claim: Friendly microbes living on the skin occupy its niches and protect against invasion by more harmful organisms.
fact_check_evidence: PMC9654002 (Skin Barrier Function and the Microbiome): commensal staphylococci secrete antimicrobial peptides that inhibit S. aureus colonization. (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9654002)
